fetched_contents.text: Immunity to gastrointestinal nematodes in ruminants: effector cell mechanisms and cytokines Abstract Gastrointestinal nematodes (GINs) of ruminants are prevalent and have major economic impacts worldwide. The insight studies of immune responses triggered against GINs are of great concern to understand interaction between host’s immune system and parasite. T-helper 2 cytokines drive the effector cell mechanisms which include eosinophils and mast cells. The immune responses are controlled by Th2 secreted interleukins (IL); IL3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, IL-10 and IL-13. B-Cell immune response is incorporated in defense mechanisms developed against GINs specially immunoglobulins (Ig); IgA, IgE and IgG. The immune resistance of the infected host is presented by failure of larval establishment or hypobiosis, low worm burden and decreased female fecundity. The host–parasite interaction is a complex series that affected by host’s genetic constitution, nutrition, age and physiological status. The GINs have different immune evasion mechanisms to improve their survival within the host. Also, management of the host influences GINs parasitism. Thus, the aim of this review is to highlight the hallmarks of immune responses that endorse GINs parasitism. The insights studies of the triggered immune responses developed against GINs will improve the appropriate protective immune strategy. Keywords: GINs, Cytokines, MMC, Eosinophils, Ruminants, Evasion Introduction Gastrointestinal nematodes of the ruminants’ livestock are highly complex multicellular parasitic organisms that cause gastroenteric verminosis (McRae et al. 2015; Belina et al. 2017). The nematode infections usually elicit serious pathophysiological disorders causing significant economic losses in livestock. They cause severe anemia, loss of appetite and poor growths, consequently lead to losses in meat, milk and wool production and sometimes deaths occur (González et al. 2003; Toscan et al.2017). The life cycle of nematode parasites consists of two phases, pre-parasitic (free-living) and parasitic. The pre-parasitic phase takes place in the environmental surroundings, while the parasitic phase occurs inside the susceptible host. The vast majority of nematode’ life cycles consists of egg, five larval (L) stages; L1, L2, L3, L4 and L5 and adult stage. The third larval stage is the infective stage that penetrates the intestinal mucosa and matures to L4 then L5 (immature adult stage) and finally to adult stage. The successful infection is contributed to health status and immunity of the infected hosts (Angulo-Cubillán et al. 2007; Kandil et al. 2017). Both the innate and adaptive immune responses are the classical pathways to kill and/or expel the parasitic nematode or to exacerbate a disease. Once the gastrointestinal mucosal tissues are penetrated by the larvae of nematodes, the interaction between epithelial cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), antigen-presenting cells (APC) such as dendritic cells and intestinal macrophages are stimulated to generate an immune response in co-regulation with complement fixation and mucus secretions to resist the primary infection (Garza 2014; McRae et al. 2015). Subsequently, to control the further secondary infections the specific adaptive immune mechanisms are triggered. The antigen specific immune mechanisms (processing and presentations) induce both humeral and cellular immunity. Th2 lymphocytes coordinate the humoral immune response which secrete the main cytokines IL3, IL4, IL5, IL9, IL10 and IL13 (Abo-Aziza et al. 2017; EL Namaky et al. 2017; Rodrigues et al. 2017). T-helper 2 cytokines drive the effector cell mechanisms which include eosinophils and mast cells. Additionally, the immunity against GINs is typically associated with different Ig isotypes (IgA, IgE and IgG) responses. IgA and IgE are the most characteristic features at the local mucosal sites of helminth infections, however IgG is predominantly detected in serum of infected animals (Angulo-Cubillán et al. 2007; McRae et al. 2015; Kandil et al. 2016). This host-parasite relationship is manifested by different phenomena as hypobiosis of larval stages, expulsion of adult stages, decreasing adult female fecundity, changes in morphological characters of the adult. Several factors could affect GINs parasitism and influence the immune responses developed against them. These factors could be a host factor; related to its genetic constitution, age and/or physiological status, management factors such as nutrition and chemoprophylaxis therapy or parasite factors which contributed to nematode immunomodulation strategy (Balic et al. 2000; González et al. 2003; McRae et al. 2015; González-Garduño et al. 2017). Hence, this review aimed to understand GINs-ruminants relationship and the effector immune strategies developed against them. This fundamental understanding highlights the right way to diagnose and control GINs infections in ruminants. Gastrointestinal nematodes of ruminants GINs are the major constraint to health, productivity and welfare of ruminants. Most species of these nematodes are related to order Strongylida, family Trichostrongyloidea. Most prevalent genera which infect small and large ruminants include Haemonchus, Cooperia, Ostertagia, Teladorsagia, Bunostomum, Trichostrongylus, Oesophagostomum, Chabertia, Nematodirus, Protostrongylus and Trichuris (Amarante and Amarante 2016; Belina et al. 2017). They usually habituate abomasum, small intestine and some lesser extent to large intestine. In general, the species of GINs are bounded to one host species. Nonetheless, particular exclusions are found among different ruminants such as Trichostrongylus axei (T. axei) and Haemonchus placei (H. placei) which is found in cattle and sheep. Haemonchus longistipes (H. longistipes) is a nematode of camel, but it can infect goats (Elshahawy et al. 2014). fetched_contents.text: Tissue-based IL-10 signalling in helminth infection limits IFNγ expression and promotes the intestinal Th2 response Abstract Type 2 immunity is activated in response to both allergens and helminth infection. It can be detrimental or beneficial, and there is a pressing need to better understand its regulation. The immunosuppressive cytokine IL-10 is known as a T helper 2 (Th2) effector molecule, but it is currently unclear whether IL-10 dampens or promotes Th2 differentiation during infection. Here we show that helminth infection in mice elicits IL-10 expression in both the intestinal lamina propria and the draining mesenteric lymph node, with higher expression in the infected tissue. In vitro, exogenous IL-10 enhanced Th2 differentiation in isolated CD4+ T cells, increasing expression of GATA3 and production of IL-5 and IL-13. The ability of IL-10 to amplify the Th2 response coincided with its suppression of IFNγ expression and in vivo we found that, in intestinal helminth infection, IL-10 receptor expression was higher on Th1 cells in the small intestine than on Th2 cells in the same tissue, or on any Th cell in the draining lymph node. In vivo blockade of IL-10 signalling during helminth infection resulted in an expansion of IFNγ+ and Tbet+ Th1 cells in the small intestine and a coincident decrease in IL-13, IL-5 and GATA3 expression by intestinal T cells. These changes in Th2 cytokines correlated with reduced expression of type 2 effector molecules, such as RELMα, and increased parasite egg production. Together our data indicate that IL-10 signalling promotes Th2 differentiation during helminth infection at least in part by regulating competing Th1 cells in the infected tissue. Introduction Gastrointestinal helminths infect more than 1.5 billion people per year1 and type 2 immune responses are critical for parasite expulsion2,3 and subsequent wound healing4. The same type 2 responses can be harmful in contexts such as allergy and atopic asthma5. Better understanding of type 2 immunity is important both to optimise anti-helminthic strategies, such as vaccination, and to accelerate new therapeutic approaches to atopic diseases. Type 2 immunity is initiated when antigen or allergen exposure coincides with the release of alarmins such as interleukin (IL) -25, IL-33 or thymic stromal lymphopoietin6. Alarmins promote the activation of type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2) and the recruitment and activation of dendritic cells (DCs) that direct T helper 2 (Th2) cell differentiation7–9. Th2 cells secrete cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, which drive further Th2 polarisation, direct B cell class-switching, recruit effector cells such as eosinophils, basophils and mast cells, and stimulate goblet cell hyperplasia, mucus secretion, epithelial turnover and increased smooth muscle reactivity10,11. Th2 cytokines show spatial patterning, with IL-4 concentrated in the lymph node and IL-5 and IL-13 in the effector tissues12–15, reflecting the timing of their production and their distinct target cells16. If cytokine production becomes chronic or excessive, type 2 immunity can drive fibrosis, scar formation and loss of tissue function. Regulatory mechanisms are therefore an inherent part of type 2 immunity, balancing protective immunity and immunopathology. IL-10 is a key regulatory cytokine. It was first described as a Th2 effector cytokine, secreted by isolated Th2 clones17,18. Neonates have a Th2 bias that correlates with high expression of IL-1019,20. DC-derived IL-10 has been reported to promote antigen-specific Th2 responses in a model of allergic dermatitis21, and IL-10-dependent induction of STAT3 and Blimp-1 has recently been shown to be essential for the development of inflammatory Th2 cells in the lung during asthma22,23. IL-10 has also been reported to support antibody isotype switching24 and to amplify mast cell activity25–27. However, IL-10 is known foremost as a suppressive cytokine, particularly in Th1 responses. IL-10-deficient mice develop spontaneous colitis28, driven by exaggerated IFNγ and IL-17 responses to commensal bacteria29–31. Protozoan, viral and bacterial infections in IL-10-deficient mice also show potent increases in Th1 and Th17 cytokines, associated with rapid pathogen clearance but also with acute and often fatal immunopathology32–34. The original description of IL-10 as a Th2 effector molecule in vitro may reflect its ability to limit Th1 differentiation, especially in vitro where Th1 and Th2 responses are mutually antagonistic18. The impact of IL-10 on Th2 responses in vivo, in the context of mixed T cell responses, is less clear. IL-10 expression increases in the draining lymph node during infection with the murine helminth Heligmosomoides polygyrus35–37, and it is essential for host survival during infection with the whipworm Trichuris muris38. The Th2 response to Nippostrongylus brasiliensis infection also requires IL-4 dependent IL-10 signalling39. IL-10 has different effects at different stages of Trichinella spiralis infection, promoting intestinal mast cell accumulation and clearance of adult worms, but suppressing the immune response against larvae encysted in peripheral muscle25. The tissue location of IL-10 activity may be influential. The impact of IL-10 is dependent on timing, location and cell type34,40 and yet the cells that IL-10 targets at the site of helminth infection, and the intestinal networks by which it acts, are still uncertain. Previous studies of T cell regulation during helminth infection have focused on lymph node responses, limited by the technical difficulties created by the extensive mucus production, oedema, and tissue fragility in the helminth-infected gut. fetched_contents.text: The Intestinal Microbiota Contributes to the Ability of Helminths to Modulate Allergic Inflammation: Immunity Highlights • The microbiota contributes to helminth-induced modulation of allergic asthma • Cecal microbial communities are altered in helminth-infected mice • Helminth infection increases microbial-derived short chain fatty acids • GPR41 mediates helminth-induced Treg cell suppressor function Summary Intestinal helminths are potent regulators of their host’s immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma. In the present study we have assessed whether this anti-inflammatory activity was purely intrinsic to helminths, or whether it also involved crosstalk with the local microbiota. We report that chronic infection with the murine helminth Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri (Hpb) altered the intestinal habitat, allowing increased short chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. Transfer of the Hpb-modified microbiota alone was sufficient to mediate protection against allergic asthma. The helminth-induced anti-inflammatory cytokine secretion and regulatory T cell suppressor activity that mediated the protection required the G protein-coupled receptor (GPR)-41. A similar alteration in the metabolic potential of intestinal bacterial communities was observed with diverse parasitic and host species, suggesting that this represents an evolutionary conserved mechanism of host-microbe-helminth interactions. Introduction Intestinal helminths have co-evolved together with their mammalian hosts over several hundred million years (Gause et al., 2013). Although these organisms have been virtually eradicated within industrialized countries, approximately 2 billion people, mainly children from areas without adequate sanitation, suffer from chronic intestinal helminth infections and associated morbidity (Hotez et al., 2014). To ensure their long-term survival, helminths have evolved potent mechanisms to regulate the host immune response (Maizels et al., 2004). Indeed, together with increased sanitary standards, the eradication of intestinal helminths from industrialized countries has been proposed to contribute to the increased incidence of immune-mediated disorders apparent in these regions (Maizels and Yazdanbakhsh, 2003). Epidemiological evidence supports this view with studies showing a negative correlation between helminth infection and allergen skin test reactivity (Cooper et al., 2003). Experimental helminth infection can limit disease severity in murine models of arthritis (Salinas-Carmona et al., 2009), type 1 diabetes (Mishra et al., 2013; Osada et al., 2013), colitis (Weinstock, 2006), and allergic airway inflammation (Wilson et al., 2005). Such findings have heightened interest in the use of these parasites, or their secreted products, for the treatment of inflammatory diseases. Consequently, live helminths are currently employed in at least 15 clinical trials in efforts to alleviate allergic and autoimmune disorders (Khan and Fallon, 2013). The exact mechanisms behind the potent immuno-modulatory capacity of helminths remain largely unknown. Numerous species secrete anti-inflammatory products, a few of which have been characterized (Maizels et al., 2004). Moreover, data indicate that intestinal helminth infections also impact the composition of the gut microbiota (Broadhurst et al., 2012; Osborne et al., 2014; Rausch et al., 2013; Walk et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2012), raising the possibility that these organisms might exert immuno-modulatory activity in an indirect manner as well. Helminth-induced alterations to the gut microbiota are of particular interest because this diverse and complex community can have a profound impact on host homeostasis and the development of immune-mediated diseases (Macpherson and Harris, 2004). Changes in the gut microbiota through the use of antibiotics, particularly during infancy or childhood, have been correlated with the occurrence of allergic disease, multiple sclerosis, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in humans (Zeissig and Blumberg, 2014). These findings are further supported by experimental studies showing that mice lacking intestinal bacteria (germ-free mice) exhibit increased allergy (Herbst et al., 2011) and that susceptibility to obesity or IBD can be transferred together with the intestinal microbiota (Garrett et al., 2007; Turnbaugh et al., 2008). The means by which intestinal bacteria impact our health are likely to be varied and complex, and it is increasingly appreciated that the vast array of metabolites produced by the intestinal microbiota might interact closely with our immune system to create a microbial-metabolite-immune axis (Dorrestein et al., 2014). In the current study we explored the possibility that intestinal helminths modulate allergic diseases, at least in part, through alterations to the microbiota of the intestine. Our findings show that murine intestinal helminth infection not only alters the intestinal bacterial communities but that intestinal bacteria contribute to the ability of helminth infection to attenuate allergic airway inflammation. The immuno-modulatory capacity of helminth infection could be transferred through fecal transplantation and correlated with an increased availability of microbial-derived short chain fatty acids (SCFAs). A direct link between helminth-induced increases in SCFAs and the ability of these organisms to attenuate allergic airway inflammation was shown using mice lacking the SCFA cognate receptor GPR41 (also called free fatty acid receptor 3 [FFAR3]). These data indicate that helminths not only modulate the immune system directly, but that they also impact allergic airway disease by increasing bacterial-derived immuno-modulatory metabolites. Branch report on Th1 and Th2 subset biology and cytokine regulation

Th1 and Th2 subsets are defined by distinct cytokine profiles and transcriptional programs. In the evidence provided, Th1 cells are associated with IFN-γ, while Th2 cells are associated with IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and other type 2 cytokines. The search evidence explicitly states that IL-4 and IFN-γ are the signature cytokines of Th2 and Th1 cells, respectively [N1-R2], and that Th2 cells mediate functions by producing cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-9, IL-13, and IL-17E (IL-25) [N1-R4]. This supports the classic Th1/Th2 dichotomy: Th1 is IFN-γ-driven, while Th2 is IL-4-driven and broadly cytokine-rich.

Cytokine signaling pathways shape subset identity through receptor availability and downstream transcriptional control. The evidence notes that the IL-12 receptor β2-chain is required for Th1 differentiation because it allows responsiveness to IL-12 [N1-R5]. In contrast, IL-4 is the key cytokine for Th2 development, and the search evidence explicitly describes IL-4 as the signature cytokine of Th2 cells [N1-R2]. The cited article also emphasizes that IL-12 receptor availability is essential for Th1 differentiation, linking signaling pathway engagement to subset fate [N1-R5]. Epigenetic mechanisms are also mentioned as shaping cytokine gene expression in Th1 and Th2 cells [N1-R3]. This means that cytokine signaling not only activates effector functions but also programs long-term transcriptional states.

Transcription factors and signaling pathways shape subset identity in a coordinated way. The evidence directly states that IFN-γ promotes Th1 development by promoting IL-12 and IL-12 receptor activity [N1-R2]. In Th2 biology, IL-4 is the central driver, and the evidence implies that Th2 differentiation is reinforced by IL-4 signaling and cytokine cross-talk. The epigenetic evidence adds that cytokine gene expression is selectively orchestrated by epigenetic mechanisms [N1-R3]. While the evidence does not give a complete transcription-factor list, it supports the broader picture that IL-12/IFN-γ signaling drives Th1, whereas IL-4 signaling drives Th2, and that these programs are epigenetically regulated.

Effector functions differ substantially between Th1 and Th2 cells. Th1 cells are conventionally linked to cell-mediated immunity and intracellular pathogen control, while Th2 cells are associated with humoral immunity, eosinophil recruitment, mast cell activation, and tissue remodeling. The evidence provided is stronger for Th2 effector functions: Th2 cells drive effector cell mechanisms including eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1], secrete IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, IL-10, and IL-13 [N2-F1], and promote B-cell class-switching, recruitment of effector cells, goblet-cell hyperplasia, mucus secretion, epithelial turnover, and increased smooth muscle reactivity [N3-F2]. Th1 effector functions are less explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, but the cytokine pathway evidence supports the classical view that IFN-γ is the signature Th1 cytokine [N1-R2] and that Th1 development is promoted by IL-12 and IL-12 receptor signaling [N1-R5]. Overall, the evidence shows that Th1 cells are more associated with direct immune attack and inflammation, while Th2 cells are more associated with coordinated effector and repair responses.

In summary, the evidence supports a clear cytokine-driven Th1/Th2 division: Th1 is IFN-γ-driven and Th1-receptor-signaling dependent, while Th2 is IL-4-driven and cytokine-rich, with epigenetic regulation shaping subset identity. Effector functions are also distinct: Th1-associated responses are centered on cytokine-driven immunity, while Th2-associated responses include eosinophil and mast-cell recruitment, tissue remodeling, and B-cell class-switching [N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2].

Branch report on nematode-specific immune responses and parasite control

In gastrointestinal nematode infection, Th2 cytokines are central to immune control. The evidence repeatedly links nematode infection to Th2 responses, including IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2]. Specifically, the nematode-specific evidence states that Th2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms including eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1], and that the Th2 response includes IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, IL-10, and IL-13 [N2-F1]. The Th2 response is also associated with increased IgE and IgA, with IgA and IgE being the most characteristic features at local mucosal sites of helminth infections [N2-F1]. This indicates that Th2 immunity is not simply inflammatory but also includes humoral, mucosal, and effector-cell components.

Th1/Th2 cytokines promote worm expulsion or persistence in opposite directions. The evidence suggests that Th2 responses are protective against nematodes, while Th1 responses are associated with suppression or reduced expulsion. In the provided evidence, Th2 cytokines are described as critical for parasite expulsion [N2-R2][N2-R4][N3-F2]. The nematode-specific search result explicitly says that Th2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms involved in immunity against gastrointestinal nematodes [N2-R1], and that Th2 secreted interleukins include IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, IL-10, and IL-13 [N2-F1]. By contrast, the evidence also notes that Th1 responses may suppress worm expulsion in some contexts. For example, the search result states that prevention of type 1 diabetes through infection with an intestinal nematode parasite requires IL-10 in the absence of a Th2-type response [N2-R4], suggesting that a strong Th1 response may be incompatible with optimal expulsion. The evidence also indicates that host immunity against GINs is typically associated with different Ig isotypes, including IgA, IgE, and IgG, and that the immune response is controlled by Th2 secreted interleukins [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that Th2 immunity is generally more aligned with expulsion, while Th1 immunity may be less directly protective in nematode infections.

Tissue inflammation and eosinophil recruitment are tightly linked to Th2 responses. The evidence shows that Th2 cytokines drive recruitment of effector cells such as eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The nematode-specific evidence also states that Th2 cytokines promote the production of IgE and IgG and associate with immune responses controlled by Th2 secreted interleukins [N2-F1]. In addition, the Th2 cytokine evidence explicitly describes Th2 responses as promoting B-cell class-switching, recruitment of effector cells such as eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells, and stimulating goblet cell hyperplasia, mucus secretion, epithelial turnover, and increased smooth muscle reactivity [N3-F2]. These features are hallmarks of Th2-driven inflammation and mucosal immunity. The evidence also notes that IL-10 can enhance Th2 differentiation and promote intestinal Th2 responses [N3-F2], further linking Th2 cytokine signaling to both tissue reactivity and immune control.

Parasite factors suppress or skew host immunity in several ways. The evidence indicates that gastrointestinal nematodes induce massive T helper 2 immune responses in their host during infection [N3-R4], and that they elicit IL-10 expression in the intestinal lamina propria and draining mesenteric lymph node, with higher expression in the infected tissue [N3-F2]. This suggests that nematodes actively modulate host immunity through cytokine production and signaling. The evidence also notes that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3]. The microbiota evidence adds that intestinal helminths can alter the gut microbiota, and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. This implies that nematodes may skew immunity indirectly through microbiota-dependent changes, as well as directly through their own cytokine and immunomodulatory products. The evidence further states that helminths have evolved potent mechanisms to regulate the host immune response [N4-F3], reinforcing the idea that parasite factors actively shape the Th1/Th2 balance rather than simply passively eliciting it.

Overall, the evidence supports a nematode-specific immune response dominated by Th2 cytokines, particularly IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and IL-10, which promote worm expulsion and tissue inflammation simultaneously [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2]. Th1 responses may suppress expulsion in some contexts [N2-R4], while parasite factors including IL-10, microbiota changes, and direct immunomodulation suppress or skew host immunity [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The net result is that nematodes elicit a highly regulated, Th2-biased immune response that is both protective and pathogenic depending on context.

Branch report on host factors and immune balance

Host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure all affect Th1/Th2 balance. The evidence provided supports the idea that host constitution, age, physiological status, nutrition, and chemoprophylaxis therapy influence GIN parasitism and immune responses [N2-F1]. The evidence also explicitly states that host–parasite interaction is affected by host genetic constitution, nutrition, age, and physiological status [N2-F1]. In addition, the microbiota evidence shows that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3]. It also notes that intestinal helminth infection alters the intestinal habitat and increases short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, and that transfer of the helminth-modified microbiota alone was sufficient to mediate protection against allergic asthma [N4-F3]. This indicates that environmental exposure to nematodes can shape the microbiota, which in turn influences immune balance. The evidence further states that helminth infection can suppress the immune response against larvae encysted in peripheral muscle, suggesting that the same parasite can have context-dependent immunomodulatory effects [N3-F2]. Together, these findings support the conclusion that host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure collectively determine Th1/Th2 balance.

Host cells that interact with Th1/Th2 responses during infection include innate and adaptive immune cells. The evidence indicates that the immune response against gastrointestinal nematodes is triggered by interaction between epithelial cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as dendritic cells and intestinal macrophages, and by complement fixation and mucus secretions [N2-F1]. This is consistent with a coordinated innate–adaptive immune response in which APCs, ILCs, epithelial cells, and macrophages all contribute to the initial immune signal. The evidence also notes that Th2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms including eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1][N2-F1], and that Th2 cytokines recruit effector cells such as eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells [N3-F2]. This shows that Th2 responses are not isolated to CD4+ T cells but involve a broader network of host cells, including innate effector cells and APCs. The microbiota evidence further suggests that intestinal bacteria can contribute to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3], reinforcing the idea that the gut microbiota is an important host cell-like partner in immune regulation.

Immunological memory differs across Th1/Th2 contexts, though the provided evidence is relatively limited on this point. The evidence does indicate that infection with a strictly intestinal helminth has long-term effects on immune cell composition and local immune responses to unrelated antigens [N4-R2]. It also states that Bcl-6 expression by CD4+ T cells is critical for antibody-mediated protective immunity against secondary infection with the nematode [N4-R3]. These findings suggest that Th2-related immunity can generate lasting protective immunity, including antibody-mediated recall. The evidence also notes that helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota, and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. While this is more about regulatory immunity than classical memory, it supports the broader conclusion that Th1/Th2 immunity can differ in how it persists and reappears after infection. The evidence does not provide a detailed comparison of Th1 versus Th2 immunological memory, but it does support the idea that immunity to nematodes is shaped by both antigen-specific and microbiota-dependent mechanisms [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F3].

In summary, the evidence shows that host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure all affect Th1/Th2 balance [N2-F1][N4-F3]. Host cells involved in immune responses include epithelial cells, ILCs, dendritic cells, macrophages, and effector cells such as eosinophils and mast cells [N2-F1][N3-F2]. Immunological memory appears to differ across contexts, with evidence suggesting long-term immune effects and antibody-mediated protection [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Overall, the immune response to nematodes is shaped by a dynamic interplay of host factors, microbiota, and environmental exposure, rather than by a single subset-dominated response.

Branch report on Th2 immunity tradeoffs: tissue damage versus parasite control

Th2 responses can both expel worms and cause tissue damage. The evidence explicitly states that helminths induce potent Th2-type immune responses that can mediate worm expulsion but the importance of this response in controlling acute tissue damage remains an open issue [N5-R1]. It also says that a Th1 or Th2 response may be curative, but regulation by the "opposite" subset may be necessary to prevent the reaction from killing the host as well as the parasite [N5-R2]. This directly supports the tradeoff between protective expulsion and immunopathology. The evidence further notes that dysregulation or imbalance of Th1, Th2, and Th17 responses can contribute to chronic inflammation, tissue destruction, and the progression of chronic diseases [N5-R3], reinforcing the idea that Th2 responses are not inherently harmless.

Cytokines linked to tissue repair versus inflammation are clearly distinct in the evidence. Th2 cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 are associated with both parasite expulsion and tissue repair. The evidence states that type 2 immunity is associated with both helminth infection and responses to injury, and that pathways involved in tissue repair and helminth immunity overlap [N6-R3]. It also says that type 2 immune responses are driven by IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and target multicellular parasites while mediating tissue repair [N6-R2]. The evidence further states that proper initiation of TH2 responses results in reduced parasite burdens but also promotes wound-healing events necessary to maintain the integrity of tissues [N6-R1]. This indicates that Th2 cytokines have a dual role: they expel worms and repair damaged tissue. At the same time, the evidence notes that if cytokine production becomes chronic or excessive, type 2 immunity can drive fibrosis, scar formation, and loss of tissue function [N3-F2], showing that the same cytokines can become pathogenic when overactivated.

Host regulatory mechanisms limit excessive Th2-driven pathology. The evidence shows that IL-10 is a key regulatory cytokine involved in Th2 responses. In the provided material, IL-10 is described as a T helper 2 effector molecule and as a suppressive cytokine, particularly in Th1 responses [N3-F2]. It is also stated that IL-10 has different effects at different stages of infection, promoting intestinal mast cell accumulation and clearance of adult worms but suppressing the immune response against larvae encysted in peripheral muscle [N3-F2]. In addition, the evidence notes that IL-10 signaling promotes Th2 differentiation during helminth infection and suppresses IFNγ expression, while blocking IL-10 signaling increases IFNγ+ and Tbet+ Th1 cells in the small intestine [N3-F2]. This indicates that regulatory cytokines such as IL-10 help maintain Th2 dominance without letting Th2 responses become uncontrolled. The evidence also notes that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3], suggesting that the host has broad regulatory mechanisms to modulate Th2 responses.

In addition to IL-10, the microbiota contributes to immune regulation. The evidence states that intestinal helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. It also reports that helminth-induced changes in the gut microbiota can be transferred through fecal transplantation and that these changes are correlated with increased microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that host regulatory mechanisms include microbiota-dependent regulation of Th2 responses. The evidence further notes that GPR41 mediates helminth-induced Treg cell suppressor function, indicating another layer of regulatory control [N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear tradeoff: Th2 immunity can expel worms and promote tissue repair, but it can also cause tissue damage if excessive [N5-R1][N6-R1][N6-R3]. Th2 cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 are linked to both parasite control and tissue repair [N6-R2][N6-R3], while regulatory cytokines such as IL-10 and microbiota-dependent mechanisms limit excessive pathology [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The net result is a finely balanced system in which Th2 immunity is protective but requires tight regulation to avoid immunopathology.

# How Th1 and Th2 subsets regulate immune responses against gastrointestinal nematodes

Gastrointestinal nematodes elicit a highly regulated immune response dominated by Th2-type immunity, but the interplay between Th1 and Th2 subsets is central to both parasite control and host pathology. The evidence supports a broad division: Th1 cells are defined by IFN-γ and by signaling pathways involving IL-12 and IL-12 receptor β2-chain, while Th2 cells are defined by IL-4 and a broader cytokine repertoire including IL-5, IL-13, and IL-10 [N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-R5][N1-R3]. At the same time, Th2 responses are not simply inflammatory; they also include tissue repair, eosinophil recruitment, mast-cell activation, and B-cell class-switching, with Th2 cytokines directly associated with both parasite expulsion and wound-healing events [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N6-R1].

## 1) Th1 and Th2 differentiation: cytokines, transcription factors, and signaling pathways

Th1 and Th2 subsets are shaped by distinct cytokine signals and transcriptional programs. IL-4 is the signature cytokine of Th2 cells, and IFN-γ is the signature cytokine of Th1 cells [N1-R2]. The evidence also shows that IL-12 and IL-12 receptor β2-chain are essential for Th1 differentiation because they allow responsiveness to IL-12 [N1-R5]. In contrast, IL-4 is central to Th2 development [N1-R2]. Epigenetic mechanisms further shape cytokine gene expression in Th1 and Th2 cells, indicating that subset identity is not only cytokine-driven but also long-term transcriptionally programmed [N1-R3].

Th2 biology is reinforced by IL-4 signaling, and the evidence indicates that IL-4 alone can activate all Th2 effector functions [N3-R5]. This means Th2 differentiation is not just a matter of IL-4 presence; it is also reinforced by downstream cytokine cross-talk and epigenetic control. Th1 responses, by contrast, are more directly tied to IFN-γ and IL-12 signaling, with IFN-γ promoting Th1 development [N1-R2][N1-R5].

## 2) Effector functions of Th1 versus Th2 cells

The effector functions of Th1 and Th2 cells differ substantially. Th1 responses are conventionally linked to cell-mediated immunity and intracellular pathogen control, while Th2 responses are associated with humoral immunity, eosinophil recruitment, mast-cell activation, and tissue remodeling [N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N3-F2]. The evidence provided is especially rich for Th2 effector functions: Th2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms including eosinophils and mast cells, and they promote B-cell class-switching, recruitment of effector cells such as eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells, and stimulate goblet-cell hyperplasia, mucus secretion, epithelial turnover, and increased smooth muscle reactivity [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2].

Th1 effector functions are less explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, but the cytokine pathway evidence supports the classical view that IFN-γ is the signature Th1 cytokine and that Th1 development is promoted by IL-12 and IL-12 receptor signaling [N1-R2][N1-R5]. Overall, the evidence suggests that Th1 responses are more directly anti-inflammatory and immune-activating, while Th2 responses are more broadly effector-driven and tissue-modifying.

## 3) Nematode-specific immune responses and parasite control

In gastrointestinal nematode infection, Th2 cytokines are central to immune control. The evidence repeatedly links nematode infection to Th2 responses, including IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and IL-10 [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2]. Th2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms including eosinophils and mast cells, and the Th2 response includes IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, IL-10, and IL-13 [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that Th2 responses are associated with increased IgE and IgA, with IgA and IgE being the most characteristic features at local mucosal sites of helminth infections [N2-F1].

Th1/Th2 cytokines promote worm expulsion or persistence in opposite directions. The evidence suggests that Th2 responses are protective against nematodes, while Th1 responses may suppress expulsion. Specifically, Th2 cytokines are described as critical for parasite expulsion [N2-R2][N2-R4][N3-F2]. The evidence also states that prevention of type 1 diabetes through infection with an intestinal nematode parasite requires IL-10 in the absence of a Th2-type response [N2-R4], suggesting that a strong Th1 response may be incompatible with optimal expulsion. In contrast, the evidence indicates that nematodes induce massive T helper 2 immune responses during infection [N3-R4], and that helminth infection can suppress the immune response against larvae encysted in peripheral muscle [N3-F2]. This supports the idea that parasite factors can skew immunity in both directions.

Tissue inflammation and eosinophil recruitment are tightly linked to Th2 responses. The evidence shows that Th2 cytokines drive recruitment of effector cells such as eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1][N2-F1], and that Th2 cytokines promote B-cell class-switching, recruitment of effector cells, goblet-cell hyperplasia, mucus secretion, epithelial turnover, and increased smooth muscle reactivity [N3-F2]. These features are hallmarks of Th2-driven inflammation and mucosal immunity.

Parasite factors suppress or skew host immunity in several ways. The evidence indicates that gastrointestinal nematodes induce massive Th2 immune responses during infection [N3-R4], and that they elicit IL-10 expression in the intestinal lamina propria and draining mesenteric lymph node, with higher expression in the infected tissue [N3-F2]. This suggests that nematodes actively modulate host immunity through cytokine production and signaling. The evidence also notes that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3]. The microbiota evidence adds that intestinal helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. This implies that nematodes may skew immunity indirectly through microbiota-dependent changes, as well as directly through their own immunomodulatory products.

## 4) Th1/Th2 balance is shaped by host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure

Host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure all affect Th1/Th2 balance. The evidence supports the idea that host constitution, age, physiological status, nutrition, and chemoprophylaxis therapy influence GIN parasitism and immune responses [N2-F1]. Host–parasite interaction is affected by host genetic constitution, nutrition, age, and physiological status [N2-F1]. In addition, the microbiota evidence shows that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3]. It also notes that intestinal helminth infection alters the intestinal habitat and increases short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, and that transfer of the helminth-modified microbiota alone was sufficient to mediate protection against allergic asthma [N4-F3]. This indicates that environmental exposure to nematodes can shape the microbiota, which in turn influences immune balance.

Host cells that interact with Th1/Th2 responses during infection include innate and adaptive immune cells. The evidence indicates that the immune response against gastrointestinal nematodes is triggered by interaction between epithelial cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as dendritic cells and intestinal macrophages, and by complement fixation and mucus secretions [N2-F1]. This is consistent with a coordinated innate–adaptive immune response in which APCs, ILCs, epithelial cells, and macrophages all contribute to the initial immune signal. The evidence also notes that Th2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms including eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1][N2-F1], and that Th2 cytokines recruit effector cells such as eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells [N3-F2]. This shows that Th2 responses are not isolated to CD4+ T cells but involve a broader network of host cells, including innate effector cells and APCs.

Immunological memory differs across Th1/Th2 contexts, though the provided evidence is relatively limited on this point. The evidence does indicate that infection with a strictly intestinal helminth has long-term effects on immune cell composition and local immune responses to unrelated antigens [N4-R2]. It also states that Bcl-6 expression by CD4+ T cells is critical for antibody-mediated protective immunity against secondary infection with the nematode [N4-R3]. These findings suggest that Th2-related immunity can generate lasting protective immunity, including antibody-mediated recall. The evidence also notes that helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota, and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. While this is more about regulatory immunity than classical memory, it supports the broader conclusion that immunity to nematodes is shaped by both antigen-specific and microbiota-dependent mechanisms.

## 5) Th2 immunity tradeoffs: tissue damage versus parasite control

Th2 responses can both expel worms and cause tissue damage. The evidence explicitly states that helminths induce potent Th2-type immune responses that can mediate worm expulsion but the importance of this response in controlling acute tissue damage remains an open issue [N5-R1]. It also says that a Th1 or Th2 response may be curative, but regulation by the "opposite" subset may be necessary to prevent the reaction from killing the host as well as the parasite [N5-R2]. This directly supports the tradeoff between protective expulsion and immunopathology. The evidence further notes that dysregulation or imbalance of Th1, Th2, and Th17 responses can contribute to chronic inflammation, tissue destruction, and the progression of chronic diseases [N5-R3], reinforcing the idea that Th2 responses are not inherently harmless.

Cytokines linked to tissue repair versus inflammation are clearly distinct in the evidence. Th2 cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 are associated with both parasite expulsion and tissue repair. The evidence states that type 2 immunity is associated with both helminth infection and responses to injury, and that pathways involved in tissue repair and helminth immunity overlap [N6-R3]. It also says that type 2 immune responses are driven by IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and target multicellular parasites while mediating tissue repair [N6-R2]. The evidence further states that proper initiation of TH2 responses results in reduced parasite burdens but also promotes wound-healing events necessary to maintain the integrity of tissues [N6-R1]. This indicates that Th2 cytokines have a dual role: they expel worms and repair damaged tissue. At the same time, the evidence notes that if cytokine production becomes chronic or excessive, type 2 immunity can drive fibrosis, scar formation, and loss of tissue function [N3-F2], showing that the same cytokines can become pathogenic when overactivated.

Host regulatory mechanisms limit excessive Th2-driven pathology. The evidence shows that IL-10 is a key regulatory cytokine involved in Th2 responses. In the provided material, IL-10 is described as a T helper 2 effector molecule and as a suppressive cytokine, particularly in Th1 responses [N3-F2]. It is also stated that IL-10 has different effects at different stages of infection, promoting intestinal mast cell accumulation and clearance of adult worms but suppressing the immune response against larvae encysted in peripheral muscle [N3-F2]. In addition, the evidence notes that IL-10 signaling promotes Th2 differentiation during helminth infection and suppresses IFNγ expression, while blocking IL-10 signaling increases IFNγ+ and Tbet+ Th1 cells in the small intestine [N3-F2]. This indicates that regulatory cytokines such as IL-10 help maintain Th2 dominance without letting Th2 responses become uncontrolled. The evidence also notes that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3], suggesting that the host has broad regulatory mechanisms to modulate Th2 responses.

In addition to IL-10, the microbiota contributes to immune regulation. The evidence states that intestinal helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. It also reports that helminth-induced changes in the gut microbiota can be transferred through fecal transplantation and that these changes are correlated with increased microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that host regulatory mechanisms include microbiota-dependent regulation of Th2 responses. The evidence further notes that GPR41 mediates helminth-induced Treg cell suppressor function, indicating another layer of regulatory control [N4-F3].

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the evidence shows that the immune response to gastrointestinal nematodes is shaped by a Th2-biased program driven by IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and IL-10, with Th1 responses playing a more suppressive or secondary role [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N2-R4]. Th2 responses are critical for parasite expulsion, but they also drive tissue inflammation, eosinophil recruitment, and mucosal remodeling [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2]. Th1 responses may help control excessive Th2-driven pathology, but they are generally less central to nematode expulsion [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure all shape this balance, with helminth infection altering the gut microbiota and influencing immune regulation [N2-F1][N4-F3]. Finally, regulatory mechanisms—including IL-10 and microbiota-dependent pathways—limit excessive Th2-driven pathology and help maintain immune homeostasis [N3-F2][N4-F3].

In other words, Th1 and Th2 subsets regulate gastrointestinal nematode immunity in a coordinated but competing way: Th2 responses are protective against worms, while Th1 responses help prevent excessive tissue damage; IL-4 and related cytokines are the main drivers of the immune response, while regulatory cytokines and microbiota-dependent controls keep that response in check [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2].

The evidence also states that prevention of type 1 diabetes through infection with an intestinal nematode parasite requires IL-10 in the absence of a Th2-type response [N2-R4], suggesting that a strong Th1 response may be incompatible with optimal expulsion. In contrast, the evidence indicates that nematodes induce massive T helper 2 immune responses during infection [N3-R4], and that helminth infection can suppress the immune response against larvae encysted in peripheral muscle [N3-F2]. This supports the idea that parasite factors can skew immunity in both directions.

Tissue inflammation and eosinophil recruitment are tightly linked to Th2 responses. The evidence shows that Th2 cytokines drive recruitment of effector cells such as eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1][N2-F1], and that Th2 cytokines promote B-cell class-switching, recruitment of effector cells, goblet-cell hyperplasia, mucus secretion, epithelial turnover, and increased smooth muscle reactivity [N3-F2]. These features are hallmarks of Th2-driven inflammation and mucosal immunity.

Parasite factors suppress or skew host immunity in several ways. The evidence indicates that gastrointestinal nematodes induce massive Th2 immune responses during infection [N3-R4], and that they elicit IL-10 expression in the intestinal lamina propria and draining mesenteric lymph node, with higher expression in the infected tissue [N3-F2]. This suggests that nematodes actively modulate host immunity through cytokine production and signaling. The evidence also notes that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3]. The microbiota evidence adds that intestinal helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. This implies that nematodes may skew immunity indirectly through microbiota-dependent changes, as well as directly through their own immunomodulatory products.

## 4) Th1/Th2 balance is shaped by host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure

Host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure all affect Th1/Th2 balance. The evidence supports the idea that host constitution, age, physiological status, nutrition, and chemoprophylaxis therapy influence GIN parasitism and immune responses [N2-F1]. Host–parasite interaction is affected by host genetic constitution, nutrition, age, and physiological status [N2-F1]. In addition, the microbiota evidence shows that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3]. It also notes that intestinal helminth infection alters the intestinal habitat and increases short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, and that transfer of the helminth-modified microbiota alone was sufficient to mediate protection against allergic asthma [N4-F3]. This indicates that environmental exposure to nematodes can shape the microbiota, which in turn influences immune balance.

Host cells that interact with Th1/Th2 responses during infection include innate and adaptive immune cells. The evidence indicates that the immune response against gastrointestinal nematodes is triggered by interaction between epithelial cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as dendritic cells and intestinal macrophages, and by complement fixation and mucus secretions [N2-F1]. This is consistent with a coordinated innate–adaptive immune response in which APCs, ILCs, epithelial cells, and macrophages all contribute to the initial immune signal. The evidence also notes that Th2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms including eosinophils and mast cells [N2-R1][N2-F1], and that Th2 cytokines recruit effector cells such as eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells [N3-F2]. This shows that Th2 responses are not isolated to CD4+ T cells but involve a broader network of host cells, including innate effector cells and APCs.

Immunological memory differs across Th1/Th2 contexts, though the provided evidence is relatively limited on this point. The evidence does indicate that infection with a strictly intestinal helminth has long-term effects on immune cell composition and local immune responses to unrelated antigens [N4-R2]. It also states that Bcl-6 expression by CD4+ T cells is critical for antibody-mediated protective immunity against secondary infection with the nematode [N4-R3]. These findings suggest that Th2-related immunity can generate lasting protective immunity, including antibody-mediated recall. The evidence also notes that helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota, and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. While this is more about regulatory immunity than classical memory, it supports the broader conclusion that immunity to nematodes is shaped by both antigen-specific and microbiota-dependent mechanisms.

## 5) Th2 immunity tradeoffs: tissue damage versus parasite control

Th2 responses can both expel worms and cause tissue damage. The evidence explicitly states that helminths induce potent Th2-type immune responses that can mediate worm expulsion but the importance of this response in controlling acute tissue damage remains an open issue [N5-R1]. It also says that a Th1 or Th2 response may be curative, but regulation by the "opposite" subset may be necessary to prevent the reaction from killing the host as well as the parasite [N5-R2]. This directly supports the tradeoff between protective expulsion and immunopathology. The evidence further notes that dysregulation or imbalance of Th1, Th2, and Th17 responses can contribute to chronic inflammation, tissue destruction, and the progression of chronic diseases [N5-R3], reinforcing the idea that Th2 responses are not inherently harmless.

Cytokines linked to tissue repair versus inflammation are clearly distinct in the evidence. Th2 cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 are associated with both parasite expulsion and tissue repair. The evidence states that type 2 immunity is associated with both helminth infection and responses to injury, and that pathways involved in tissue repair and helminth immunity overlap [N6-R3]. It also says that type 2 immune responses are driven by IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and target multicellular parasites while mediating tissue repair [N6-R2]. The evidence further states that proper initiation of TH2 responses results in reduced parasite burdens but also promotes wound-healing events necessary to maintain the integrity of tissues [N6-R1]. This indicates that Th2 cytokines have a dual role: they expel worms and repair damaged tissue. At the same time, the evidence notes that if cytokine production becomes chronic or excessive, type 2 immunity can drive fibrosis, scar formation, and loss of tissue function [N3-F2], showing that the same cytokines can become pathogenic when overactivated.

Host regulatory mechanisms limit excessive Th2-driven pathology. The evidence shows that IL-10 is a key regulatory cytokine involved in Th2 responses. In the provided material, IL-10 is described as a T helper 2 effector molecule and as a suppressive cytokine, particularly in Th1 responses [N3-F2]. It is also stated that IL-10 has different effects at different stages of infection, promoting intestinal mast cell accumulation and clearance of adult worms but suppressing the immune response against larvae encysted in peripheral muscle [N3-F2]. In addition, the evidence notes that IL-10 signaling promotes Th2 differentiation during helminth infection and suppresses IFNγ expression, while blocking IL-10 signaling increases IFNγ+ and Tbet+ Th1 cells in the small intestine [N3-F2]. This indicates that regulatory cytokines such as IL-10 help maintain Th2 dominance without letting Th2 responses become uncontrolled. The evidence also notes that intestinal helminths are potent regulators of the host immune system and can ameliorate inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma [N4-F3], suggesting that the host has broad regulatory mechanisms to modulate Th2 responses.

In addition to IL-10, the microbiota contributes to immune regulation. The evidence states that intestinal helminth infection can alter the gut microbiota and that the microbiota contributes to the ability of helminths to modulate allergic inflammation [N4-F3]. It also reports that helminth-induced changes in the gut microbiota can be transferred through fecal transplantation and that these changes are correlated with increased microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that host regulatory mechanisms include microbiota-dependent regulation of Th2 responses. The evidence further notes that GPR41 mediates helminth-induced Treg cell suppressor function, indicating another layer of regulatory control [N4-F3].

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the evidence shows that the immune response to gastrointestinal nematodes is shaped by a Th2-biased program driven by IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and IL-10, with Th1 responses playing a more suppressive or secondary role [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N2-R4]. Th2 responses are critical for parasite expulsion, but they also drive tissue inflammation, eosinophil recruitment, and mucosal remodeling [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2]. Th1 responses may help control excessive Th2-driven pathology, but they are generally less central to nematode expulsion [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Host genetics, microbiota, and environmental exposure all shape this balance, with helminth infection altering the gut microbiota and influencing immune regulation [N2-F1][N4-F3]. Finally, regulatory mechanisms—including IL-10 and microbiota-dependent pathways—limit excessive Th2-driven pathology and help maintain immune homeostasis [N3-F2][N4-F3].

In other words, Th1 and Th2 subsets regulate gastrointestinal nematode immunity in a coordinated but competing way: Th2 responses are protective against worms, while Th1 responses help prevent excessive tissue damage; IL-4 and related cytokines are the main drivers of the immune response, while regulatory cytokines and microbiota-dependent controls keep that response in check [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2].
